cards.h: How politics was studied before the 1950s
cards.b:
An approach is a way of looking. It decides what questions you ask and what evidence you use.

Before the Second World War, political science mostly used traditional approaches. These were value-based, used history and law, and focused on the state and its institutions.

This is the oldest approach. It starts with values and reasoning, not data. It asks: what is the ideal state, and what is justice?

  • Thinkers: Plato, Aristotle, Hegel, T.H. Green.
  • Strength: it gives us goals and ideals to aim for.
  • Weakness: it can be abstract and hard to test. Critics say it is speculative.

This approach says you can only understand political ideas in their historical setting. Ideas come from real problems of their age.

  • Thinkers: Machiavelli used history as a tool; Sabine and Dunning wrote histories of political thought.
  • Strength: it gives context. Hobbes makes more sense when you know about the English Civil War.
  • Weakness: history can be read selectively, and the past does not always predict the present.

This approach studies formal structures: constitutions, legislatures, executives and courts.

  • Thinkers: James Bryce (Modern Democracies), Herman Finer, Harold Laski.
  • Strength: it is concrete and descriptive. It is good for comparing governments.
  • Weakness: it ignores informal politics like caste, pressure groups and personality. A constitution on paper can differ a lot from politics in practice.

This approach sees the state mainly as a legal body that makes and enforces law. Politics is studied through laws, rights and courts.

  • Thinkers: Jean Bodin and Hobbes (sovereignty as the source of law), A.V. Dicey (rule of law), John Austin (law as the command of the sovereign).
  • Weakness: it is very narrow. Law is only one part of political life.

• They are value-laden: they openly judge what is good.
  • They are state-centric: the state is the main unit of study.
  • They are descriptive and prescriptive, rather than explanatory or predictive.
  • They rely on reasoning, history and legal texts, not surveys or statistics.

After 1945, American scholars felt traditional approaches could not explain real political behaviour. They could not explain why democracy collapsed in Weimar Germany or why people voted for fascists.

The criticism was that traditional approaches were too formal, too normative and too narrow. This opened the door for the behavioural revolution, which is the next lesson.

Some books add more traditional approaches.

Comparative approach

Aristotle compared 158 constitutions. Montesquieu, in The Spirit of the Laws (1748), compared laws across countries and linked them to climate, religion and customs. Bryce compared modern democracies.

Sociological approach

Studies how society shapes politics, as Montesquieu and later Tocqueville did in Democracy in America (1835–40).

Psychological approach

Graham Wallas, in Human Nature in Politics (1908), argued people act on instinct and emotion more than reason. This prepared the ground for behaviouralism.

These bridge the old and the new: they stay value-based, but begin to look at how politics actually works.
The next lesson on behaviouralism takes up the right-hand side. Use this contrast as a one-line summary in any answer on the shift in approaches.

The institutional and legal approaches still matter a lot in India. Debates on the basic structure doctrine (Kesavananda Bharati, 1973), the anti-defection law, or Governor's powers are mainly legal-institutional.

But you can only explain coalition politics or caste voting with newer approaches. A strong answer shows both.

"Critically examine the traditional approaches to the study of politics."

Structure: define approach, describe the four types with one thinker each, give common features, then the behavioural critique. End by saying modern theory has a revival of new institutionalism (March and Olsen, 1984), which shows that institutions still matter.

quiz.q:
Consider the following statements:
1. Aristotle is said to have compared 158 constitutions.
2. Montesquieu's The Spirit of the Laws (1748) compared laws only as legal codes and ignored climate, religion and customs.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
quiz.w: 1 is true: the comparative approach section says Aristotle compared 158 constitutions. 2 is false: Montesquieu linked laws to climate, religion and customs.

quiz.q:
Consider the following statements:
1. The philosophical approach starts with values and reasoning, not data.
2. The historical approach is illustrated by the work of James Bryce, who wrote Modern Democracies.
3. The legal approach sees the state mainly as a legal body that makes and enforces law.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
quiz.w: 1 is true: the philosophical approach starts with values and reasoning. 2 is false: Bryce is an institutional thinker; the historical approach used Sabine and Dunning. 3 is true: the lesson's legal approach definition.

quiz.q:
Consider the following statements:
1. Graham Wallas, in Human Nature in Politics (1908), argued that people act on instinct and emotion more than reason.
2. The institutional approach's main strength is that it covers informal politics such as caste and pressure groups.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
quiz.w: 1 is true: Wallas stressed instinct and emotion. 2 is false: the institutional approach ignores informal politics; that is its weakness, not its strength.

quiz.q:
Consider the following statements about traditional approaches:
1. They are value-laden, openly judging what is good.
2. They rely mainly on surveys and statistics.
3. They are state-centric, with the state as the main unit of study.
How many of the statements given above are correct?
quiz.w: 1 is true: they openly judge what is good. 2 is false: they rely on reasoning, history and legal texts, not surveys or statistics. 3 is true: the state is the main unit. Two are correct.

quiz.q:
Consider the following statements:
1. The historical approach gives context: Hobbes makes more sense when you know about the English Civil War.
2. John Austin defined law as the general will of the people.
3. A.V. Dicey's work is on pressure groups.
How many of the statements given above are correct?
quiz.w: 1 is true: the lesson uses Hobbes and the English Civil War as its example. 2 is false: Austin defined law as the command of the sovereign. 3 is false: Dicey is linked to the rule of law. One is correct.

quiz.q:
Consider the following pairs:
1. Institutional approach: Herman Finer and Harold Laski
2. Legal approach: Graham Wallas
3. Comparative approach: Montesquieu
How many pairs are correctly matched?
quiz.w: 1 is correct: both are institutional thinkers in the lesson. 2 is wrong: Wallas is in the psychological approach. 3 is correct: Montesquieu is in the comparative section. Two are correct.

quiz.q:
Consider the following pairs:
1. Sociological approach: Tocqueville's Democracy in America (1835-40)
2. Psychological approach: Montesquieu's The Spirit of the Laws (1748)
3. Philosophical approach: John Austin
How many pairs are correctly matched?
quiz.w: 1 is correct: the lesson links Tocqueville to the sociological approach. 2 is wrong: the psychological approach is Wallas's. 3 is wrong: Austin is in the legal approach. One is correct.

quiz.q:
Consider the following statements:
Statement-I: The institutional approach is good for comparing governments.
Statement-II: The institutional approach takes account of informal politics such as caste and pressure groups.
Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?
o: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are individually true and Statement-II is the correct explanation of Statement-I
Both Statement-I and Statement-II are individually true but Statement-II is not the correct explanation of Statement-I
Statement-I is true but Statement-II is false
Statement-I is false but Statement-II is true
quiz.w: Statement-I is true: the lesson says it is good for comparing governments. Statement-II is false: the approach ignores informal politics.

quiz.q: Which one of the following is NOT a common feature of traditional approaches, as the lesson lists them?
quiz.w: Traditional approaches rely on reasoning, history and legal texts, not surveys or statistics. The other three are listed features.

quiz.q:
Arrange these works in chronological order:
1. Montesquieu's The Spirit of the Laws
2. Tocqueville's Democracy in America
3. Graham Wallas's Human Nature in Politics
4. The Kesavananda Bharati case
Which one of the following is the correct order?
quiz.w: The years are 1748, 1835-40, 1908 and 1973 (the lesson gives 1973 for Kesavananda Bharati). So 1-2-3-4.
